newsitem.title: UK: Angerstein says wants to buy managing agents.
newsitem.headline: Angerstein says wants to buy managing agents.

text.p: Angerstein Underwriting, which last week completed the acquisition of members' agency Stace Barr Wellington, said on Wednesday it would continue to look for opportunities to expand its interest in managing agents.
The comments came as the investment trust, one of the largest corporate investors at Lloyd's of London, reported a double digit increase in half year earnings.
The long term strategy of the group was to increase its involvement in putting dedicated capital behind underwriters John Stace, chief executive of Angerstein, told Reuters. shareholdings, he added.

Stace also said that he expected the number of traditional Names at Lloyd's of London to continue to fall to a core level of between 4,000 and 5,000 with four or five companies looking after their interests.
Providing it could maintain costs, quality and manage the downside risk, he said Angerstein wanted to work towards 20 percent of that business.
The company currently represents around 950 of over 12,000 current Names at Lloyd's.
In addition to Stace Barr, Angerstein also completed the acquisition of two managing agents, Mumford and Coffey, last week.
Through these and its existing spread portfolio, it now owns, advises or manages around nine percent of Lloyd's of London's total 1997 capacity of around 10.3 billion stg.

In the six months to November 30 Angerstein's net revenue after tax rose 17.5 percent to 1.94 million stg. Earnings per share were up 17.9 percent at 1.64 pence and the interim dividend increased 9.1 percent to 1.2 pence.
The rise in earnings reflected strong growth in dividend income from equities together with the emergence of cost savings from last year's acquisition of Lloyd's investment trust Delian.
In the future the results will include underwriting income from Angerstein's recent acquisitions.
Outlining expectations for the 1994 and 1995 underwriting years, Angerstein said it anticipated returns of at least 7.5 percent of capacity for the 1994 underwriting year and 7.1 percent for 1995.
The 1994 number, based on managing agents' lowest estimates, it described as "somewhat conservative".

While too early to form any definite views about 1996, Angerstein said it drew some comfort from the relative infrequency of insured catastrophe losses in the calendar year, especially against a background of weaker market conditions.

"The market's exceedingly competitive - probably as competitive as it was in the late 1980s, though it's a very different market structure... But we're not complacent," said Angerstein operations director James Illingworth.

"We haven't increased Angerstein's capacity, and gearing has reduced every year since 1995. We were very conservative in the auction last year and spent just over 50,000 stg on quite a large remodelling of the portfolio."
The group has reduced its exposure to marine, hull and energy business to below 14 percent of its total premium income, expanding in the non-marine area.
